label: R10
title: Adaptive Optimization and Dynamic Programming
brief: Recitation 10 links adaptive (two-stage stochastic) optimization from L15 to dynamic programming from L16 through one idea: immediate cost plus optimal expected future value. A bakery example (bake at \$2 tonight, buy any shortfall at \$3 tomorrow, demand 2 or 6) is used to write the two-stage model in compact and extensive form and to compare deterministic, adaptive and wait-and-see benchmarks through VSS and EVPI. The DP half covers the five ingredients, backward induction on a decision tree, and choosing a sufficient state, worked through on the unbounded integer knapsack. The bakery is then recast as a two-stage DP, showing that the AO recourse function is the expected cost-to-go and that DP merges histories a scenario tree keeps apart. Optional slides run Bellman–Ford on a graph with a cycle and Benders decomposition by hand on the bakery.
kp: Two-stage AO: $\min_{x\in X} c^\top x+Q(x)$; first-stage $x$ is static, recourse $y_s$ adapts to each scenario.
Costs always rank $C_{DET}\ge C_{AO}\ge C_{WS}$, so VSS $=C_{DET}-C_{AO}\ge0$ and EVPI $=C_{AO}-C_{WS}\ge0$.
Bakery: $x_{AO}=2$, $C_{AO}=10$; DET bakes 4 with $Z_{DET}=8$ but $C_{DET}=11$; $C_{WS}=8$ → VSS 1, EVPI 2.
Critical fractile: bake another unit while $P(d>x)\cdot p$ exceeds the bake cost; AO can bake below the mean.
$Z_{AO}=C_{AO}$ and $Z_{WS}=C_{WS}$, but $Z_{DET}\ne C_{DET}$ in general; $Z_{DET}$ vs $Z_{WS}$ has no fixed order.
DP = stage, sufficient state, decision (+ uncertainty), transition, cost; solve the Bellman equation by backward induction.
A DP solution is a first decision plus a policy $\mu^*_t(s_t)$ for every state, not one path.
Knapsack state: $(i,s)$ for binary, $s$ alone for unbounded integer.
AO recourse $Q(x)$ = DP expected cost-to-go; DP merges histories with the same state (10 nights: 130 entries vs 1,023 tree nodes).
Bellman–Ford adds an edge-count stage to make a cyclic recursion acyclic; Benders builds $Q$ from below with cuts until LB = UB.

topics.x: The first-stage decision $x$ is fixed before uncertainty is revealed; second-stage recourse $y_s$ is chosen after observing scenario $s$. The model is $\min_{x\in X} c^\top x+Q(x)$ with $Q(x)=\sum_s\pi_sQ_s(x)$, where each $Q_s(x)$ is a recourse LP. In the bakery, linearizing $Q_s(x)=3\max\{d_s-x,0\}$ with epigraph variables gives the extensive form.

topics.n: Benchmarks: DET, AO, WS, VSS, EVPI
topics.x: DET optimizes against mean data, AO against the distribution, and WS lets $x$ depend on the scenario (clairvoyant). Comparing true expected costs gives $C_{DET}\ge C_{AO}\ge C_{WS}$, VSS $=C_{DET}-C_{AO}$ and EVPI $=C_{AO}-C_{WS}$. A model's own optimal value $Z$ equals its true cost $C$ for AO and WS but not for DET, which never sees a shortage.

A DP has stages, a sufficient state, decisions (plus uncertainty depending only on state and decision), a transition and stage costs. The Bellman equation $J_t(s)=\min_x E[f_t+J_{t+1}(g_t(s,x,u_t))]$ is solved backward from $J_T=f_T$; on a tree, decision nodes take a min and chance nodes an expectation. The output is a first decision plus a rule for every state.

The state must carry exactly the information future decisions and costs need: too little makes the recursion wrong, too much makes it expensive. Binary knapsack needs $(i,s)$, while unbounded knapsack needs only remaining capacity $s$, with $J(s)=\max\{0,\max_{j:a_j\le s}[c_j+J(s-a_j)]\}$ filled in increasing $s$. Storing the argmax lets you trace back an optimal solution.

The bakery is a two-stage DP with $s_1=x_0-u_0$ and $J_1(s_1)=3\max\{0,-s_1\}$, so $E[J_1(x_0-u_0)]$ is exactly the AO recourse function $Q(x_0)$. Scenario copies $y_s$ correspond to a policy $\mu_1^*(s_1)$. Over many periods a scenario tree grows exponentially in histories, while DP merges histories that reach the same state.

On a graph with a directed cycle the natural recursion has no computation order. Adding a stage $t$ = maximum number of edges gives $J_t(i)=\min\{J_{t-1}(i),\min_{(j,i)\in E}[J_{t-1}(j)+c(j,i)]\}$, which is acyclic. Without negative cycles $|V|-1$ stages suffice, for $O(|V||E|)$ work.

The master $\min 2x+\theta$ with $\theta\ge0$ under-approximates $Q$ with optimality cuts $\theta\ge\sum_s\pi_s\lambda_s^k(d_s-x)$ from the subproblem duals. The master value is a lower bound and the best $c^\top x^k+Q(x^k)$ an upper bound; stop when they meet. In the bakery it converges in three iterations to $x=2$, value 10.

cards.f: Static vs adaptive decision in a two-stage problem.
cards.b: Static: chosen before uncertainty is revealed, same value in every scenario (bakery $x$). Adaptive: chosen after observing it, may differ by scenario (bakery $y_L$, $y_H$).
cards.x: Making x adaptive too is wait-and-see (a clairvoyant), not AO.
$Q_s(x)$ is the optimal value of the scenario-$s$ recourse LP; $Q(x)$ is its expectation.

cards.f: Bakery: how do you get the extensive form from $Q_s(x)=3\max\{d_s-x,0\}$?
cards.b: Linearize each max with an epigraph variable: $y_s\ge d_s-x$, $y_s\ge0$, weight $\pi_s\cdot3=\tfrac32$: $\min 2x+\tfrac32y_L+\tfrac32y_H$ s.t. $y_L\ge2-x$, $y_H\ge6-x$, $0\le x\le6$.
cards.x: Minimization pushes $y_s$ down onto $\max\{d_s-x,0\}$, so the linearization is exact.

cards.b: $C_{DET}=c^\top x_{DET}+Q(x_{DET})$ with $x_{DET}$ from the mean-data model; $C_{AO}=\min_x c^\top x+Q(x)$; $C_{WS}=\sum_s\pi_s\min_x\{c^\top x+Q_s(x)\}$.
cards.x: $C$ = true expected cost of the first-stage decision; $Z$ = the model's own optimal value.

cards.f: VSS and EVPI: definitions and sign.
cards.b: VSS $=C_{DET}-C_{AO}$ (value of using the distribution); EVPI $=C_{AO}-C_{WS}$ (value of knowing the outcome first). Both $\ge0$: $x_{DET}$ is feasible for AO, and WS relaxes AO.
cards.x: Ordering that always holds (min): $C_{DET}\ge C_{AO}\ge C_{WS}$.

cards.f: Bakery results ($c=2$, morning price 3, $d\in\{2,6\}$ w.p. ½).
cards.x: Expected cost is $12-x$ on $[0,2]$ and $9+x/2$ on $[2,6]$.

cards.b: Bake another loaf while $P(d>x)\cdot p>2$ ($p$ = morning price). $p=3$: stop at 2. $p=5$: bake to 6. $p=4$: any $x\in[2,6]$.
cards.x: AO is not 'mean + safety stock': at p = 3 it bakes below the mean of 4.

cards.f: For which models does $Z=C$ always hold?
cards.b: AO and WS ($Z_{AO}=C_{AO}$, $Z_{WS}=C_{WS}$). DET generally not: bakery $Z_{DET}=8\ne C_{DET}=11$ because the mean-value model never sees a shortage.
cards.x: No fixed order of $Z_{DET}$ vs $Z_{WS}$; with only random RHS in an LP, Jensen gives $Z_{DET}\le Z_{WS}$.

cards.b: Stage $t$; state $s_t$ (sufficient summary of the past); decision $x_t\in X_t(s_t)$ plus uncertainty $u_t$ depending only on $(s_t,x_t)$; transition $s_{t+1}=g_t(s_t,x_t,u_t)$; costs $f_t$ and terminal $f_T$.
cards.x: Too little state information breaks the recursion; too much makes it expensive.
Work per stage ≈ (# states) × (# choices) × (# outcomes).

cards.f: What does backward induction on a decision tree return?
cards.b: An optimal first decision $x_0^*$ plus a rule $\mu_1^*(s_1)$ for every stage-1 state, not a single path.
cards.x: Decision nodes take a min; chance nodes take an expectation.

cards.f: Smallest sufficient state: binary vs unbounded integer knapsack.
cards.b: Binary: $(i,s)$ (item index, remaining capacity) → $n(K+1)$ entries, 2 choices each. Unbounded: $s$ alone → $K+1$ entries, $n$ choices each.
cards.x: Binary needs i to know which items are still available.

cards.f: Unbounded knapsack recursion and graph view.
cards.b: $J(s)=\max\{0,\max_{j:a_j\le s}[c_j+J(s-a_j)]\}$, $J(0)=0$; fill in increasing $s$, store the argmax, trace back from $J(K)$. Graph: arcs $s\to s-a_j$ of length $c_j$; $J(K)$ is a longest path from $K$.
cards.x: $a_j>0$ makes the graph acyclic, so increasing $s$ is a valid order.

cards.b: First-stage $x$ ↔ $x_0$ in $s_0$; scenario $s$ w.p. $\pi_s$ ↔ uncertainty $u_0$; per-scenario $y_s$ ↔ policy $\mu_1^*(s_1)$; recourse $Q(x)$ ↔ expected cost-to-go $E[J_1(s_1)]$.
cards.x: Trap: s indexes scenarios in AO but denotes the state in DP.

cards.b: $J_t(i)=\min\{J_{t-1}(i),\min_{j:(j,i)\in E}[J_{t-1}(j)+c(j,i)]\}$, $J_0(o)=0$, $J_0(i)=\infty$ otherwise; $t$ = max edges. $|V|-1$ stages suffice with no negative cycle; work $O(|V||E|)$.
cards.x: The edge-count stage makes the recursion acyclic even when the graph is not.

cards.f: Benders on the bakery: master, cuts, bounds.
cards.b: Master $\min 2x+\theta$, $0\le x\le6$, $\theta\ge0$, plus cuts $\theta\ge\sum_s\tfrac12\lambda_s^k(d_s-x)$. LB = $2x^k+\theta^k$; UB = $\min_{\tau\le k}\{2x^\tau+Q(x^\tau)\}$. Stop when LB = UB.
cards.x: Without $\theta\ge0$ the first master (no cuts) is unbounded.

quiz.q: Bakery: bake $x$ tonight before demand is known, then buy $y$ more after seeing $d$. Which decisions are adaptive?
quiz.e: $y$ is chosen after $d$ is observed, so $y_L$ and $y_H$ may differ; $x$ is fixed before. 'Both' is wait-and-see: a clairvoyant who knows $d$ tonight.

quiz.q: For a minimization problem, which ordering of true expected costs always holds?
quiz.e: $x_{DET}$ is one feasible first-stage choice for AO, so $C_{AO}\le C_{DET}$; WS lets $x$ depend on $s$, a relaxation of AO, so $C_{WS}\le C_{AO}$. WS can never cost more than AO.

quiz.q: Bakery (bake \$2, morning price \$3, $d\in\{2,6\}$ w.p. ½). DET plans for $\bar d=4$ and bakes 4. What is $C_{DET}$?
quiz.e: If $d=2$: cost 8. If $d=6$: buy 2 at \$3, cost 14. Average 11. 8 is $Z_{DET}$, the model's own value, which never sees a shortage.

quiz.q: In the same bakery, $C_{AO}=10$ and $C_{WS}=8$. What are VSS and EVPI?
quiz.e: VSS $=C_{DET}-C_{AO}=11-10=1$; EVPI $=C_{AO}-C_{WS}=10-8=2$. 3 is $C_{DET}-C_{WS}$, the sum of the two gaps.

quiz.q: The morning price rises from \$3 to \$5 (bake cost still \$2). How many loaves does AO bake tonight?
quiz.e: A loaf in $[2,6]$ saves \$5 only if $d=6$: expected $\tfrac12\cdot5=2.5>2$, so bake up to 6. 'Any $x\in[2,6]$' is the \$4 case, where $\tfrac12\cdot4=2$ exactly.

quiz.q: At a morning price of \$5, what is the EVPI of the bakery?
quiz.e: AO bakes 6, cost 12 in both scenarios, so $C_{AO}=12$. WS bakes exactly $d$ and never buys in the morning, so $C_{WS}=8$ whatever the price. EVPI $=12-8=4$; 2 is the EVPI at \$3.

quiz.q: Which pair of equalities between a model's optimal value $Z$ and its true expected cost $C$ always holds?
quiz.e: The AO and WS objectives are their true expected costs by definition. DET optimizes against mean data and never sees the shortage: bakery $Z_{DET}=8$ but $C_{DET}=11$.

quiz.q: Variant: demand is known to be 4, baking costs \$2, and the morning price is \$1 or \$5 w.p. ½. Compute $Z_{DET}$ and $Z_{WS}$.
quiz.e: DET sees the mean price \$3 > \$2 and bakes 4: 8. WS buys all 4 at \$1 in the low case (4) and bakes 4 in the high case (8): average 6. So $Z_{DET}>Z_{WS}$ here; Jensen's $Z_{DET}\le Z_{WS}$ needs randomness only in the RHS.

quiz.q: In a DP, the state $s_t$ should be:
o: A sufficient summary of the past for future decisions and costs
The full history of all past decisions and outcomes
quiz.e: Too little information makes the recursion incorrect; the full history is sufficient but needlessly expensive.

quiz.q: Option $a$ costs 1 now and leads (w.p. ½ each) to states with $J_1=4$ or $2$; option $b$ costs 3 now and leads to $J_1=1$ or $2$. What are $J_0$ and $x_0^*$?
quiz.e: $a$: $1+\tfrac12(4+2)=4$; $b$: $3+\tfrac12(1+2)=4.5$; take the min. Dropping the stage-0 cost gives 3 vs 1.5 and wrongly picks $b$.

quiz.q: Deciding knapsack items one by one, what is the smallest sufficient state for the unbounded integer knapsack?
o: The vector of quantities chosen so far
quiz.e: With unlimited copies it does not matter which items were used, only how much capacity is left. $(i,s)$ is what the binary version needs.
Items that fit: $j=2$: $7+J(0)=7$; $j=3$: $5+J(1)=6$; $j=4$: $1+J(3)=6$. Max is 7. 6 comes from starting with item 3 or 4.

quiz.q: Bake whole loaves for 10 nights; demand each night is independently 2 or 6; inventory carries over with capacity 12. How many scenario-tree decision nodes vs DP state entries (night, stock)?
quiz.e: Tree: $1+2+\dots+2^9=2^{10}-1=1{,}023$. DP: 13 stock levels (0–12) × 10 nights = 130, since many histories lead to the same stock. 20 counts nights × outcomes, not histories.

quiz.q: In the AO ↔ DP dictionary, the recourse function $Q(x)$ corresponds to:
quiz.e: In the bakery DP, $E[J_1(x_0-u_0)]$ is exactly $Q(x_0)$. The policy corresponds to the per-scenario recourse variables $y_s$, not to $Q$.

quiz.q: Arcs $o\to a$ (4), $o\to b$ (2), $b\to a$ (1), $a\to b$ (2), $a\to d$ (3), $b\to d$ (6); $J_1=(0,4,2,\infty)$ for $(o,a,b,d)$. Find $J_2(d)$ and $J_3(d)$.
quiz.e: $J_2(d)=\min\{4+3,2+6\}=7$ and $J_2(a)=\min\{4,2+1\}=3$, so $J_3(d)=\min\{7,3+3,2+6\}=6$ via $o\to b\to a\to d$. Cost 6 needs three edges, so it cannot appear at $t=2$.

quiz.q: Benders on the bakery, iteration 2 evaluates $x^2=4$ (iteration 1 gave UB = 12). What are $Q(4)$ and the new UB?
quiz.e: Only $d_H$ is short, by 2 at \$3 w.p. ½: $Q(4)=3$, so $2\cdot4+3=11<12$. $Q=0$ is the master's $\theta^2$; UB $=8$ confuses it with the LB.

quiz.q: At $x^2=4$ the subproblem duals are $\lambda_s=3$ if $x<d_s$ and $0$ if $x>d_s$. Which optimality cut is added?
quiz.e: $\lambda_L=0$ ($4>2$), $\lambda_H=3$: $\theta\ge\tfrac12\cdot3(6-x)=9-1.5x$. $12-3x$ is cut 1 (both scenarios short); $18-3x$ drops the ½; $\theta\ge3$ is a constant, not a cut valid for all $x$.

quiz.q: Which statement holds at every Benders iteration k?
o: The master is bounded even with no lower bound on $\theta$
quiz.e: Cuts under-estimate $Q$, so the master is a relaxation and its value is a lower bound. The iterate's true cost can rise (it only happens to fall in the bakery), which is why the best UB so far is reported.

written.q: Bakery: bake $x\in[0,6]$ loaves tonight at \$2; demand is 2 or 6 w.p. ½; any shortfall is bought tomorrow at price $p$; leftovers are wasted. (a) Write the AO extensive form. (b) For $p=3$, compute $x_{AO}$, $C_{AO}$, $Z_{DET}$, $C_{DET}$, $C_{WS}$, VSS and EVPI. (c) State the rule that determines how much AO bakes, find $x_{AO}$ for $p=5$, and explain why DET does not change its decision.
written.m: (a) $\min 2x+\tfrac p2y_L+\tfrac p2y_H$ s.t. $y_L\ge2-x$, $y_H\ge6-x$, $0\le x\le6$, $y_L,y_H\ge0$ (epigraph of $p\max\{d_s-x,0\}$). (b) $2x+Q(x)=12-x$ on $[0,2]$ and $9+x/2$ on $[2,6]$, so $x_{AO}=2$, $C_{AO}=10$. DET plans for $\bar d=4$, bakes 4: $Z_{DET}=8$, true cost 8 or 14, $C_{DET}=11$. WS bakes $d$: 4 or 12, $C_{WS}=8$. VSS $=1$, EVPI $=2$. (c) Critical fractile: bake another loaf while $P(d>x)\,p>2$. On $[2,6]$, $P(d>x)=\tfrac12$; at $p=5$, $2.5>2$, so $x_{AO}=6$, $C_{AO}=12$ (vs $C_{DET}=13$). DET bakes 4 for any $p>2$ because the mean-value model never sees a shortage, so the price of the recourse never enters its decision.
k: Extensive form with epigraph variables and ½ probability weights
Explains DET's insensitivity to the morning price

written.q: Unbounded integer knapsack: $\max 11x_1+7x_2+5x_3+x_4$ s.t. $6x_1+4x_2+3x_3+x_4\le25$, $x\in\mathbb{Z}^4_+$. (a) Define the DP state, decision, transition and reward. (b) Write the Bellman recursion and justify the order of computation. (c) Compute $J(0),\dots,J(6)$. (d) Why does the binary (0/1) version need a larger state, and how big is each table? (e) Given $J(25)=45$ with stored argmaxes, recover one optimal solution.
written.m: (a) State $s$ = remaining capacity; decision = next item $j$ with $a_j\le s$ (or stop); transition $s\to s-a_j$; reward $c_j$. (b) $J(s)=\max\{0,\max_{j:a_j\le s}[c_j+J(s-a_j)]\}$, $J(0)=0$. Every $a_j>0$, so transitions strictly reduce $s$ and the table can be filled for $s=0,1,\dots,25$ in increasing order (a longest path on an acyclic graph). (c) $J=0,1,2,5,7,8,11$ for $s=0..6$; e.g. $J(4)=\max\{7+0,5+1,1+5\}=7$, $J(6)=\max\{11+0,7+2,5+5,1+8\}=11$. (d) In the 0/1 version each item can be used once, so the state must record which items remain: $(i,s)$ with $n(K+1)$ entries and 2 choices each, vs $K+1$ entries with $n$ choices for the unbounded version. (e) Trace back $25\to19\to13\to7\to1\to0$ using item 1 four times and item 4 once: $x^*=(4,0,0,1)$, value 45. A tie at $s=7$ ($7\to3\to0$ via items 2 and 3) gives another optimum, $(3,1,1,0)$.
k: Correct recursion with J(0)=0 and increasing-s order justified by a_j > 0
Binary needs (i,s); table sizes n(K+1) vs K+1
